item.title: A victory for our cricket. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh Cricket Team’s historic Test victory on Australian soil deserves wholehearted congratulations.
Winning a Test in Australia is one of the hardest feats in world cricket, and for the Bangladesh team to have finally done it deserves praise.
What is most impressive is that this was not luck, nor a one‑off burst of brilliance, with the team comprehensively beating Australia in less than four days, dominating the match from the get go.
Now, we can hope for discipline, clarity, and a renewed belief in the long format of the game. Najmul Hossain Shanto’s praise for the team’s “new Test mindset” captures exactly what made this win possible.
That mindset must now become a permanent feature of Bangladesh cricket. Too often, we have treated Test cricket as an obligation rather than a priority. This must change.
The players deserve immense credit, but so do the coaches, analysts, trainers, and support staff who have worked quietly behind the scenes to instill structure and confidence.
Transforming a team’s mentality is not easy. It requires trust, consistency, and a willingness to challenge old habits. This victory is a testament to that collective effort.
Celebration however must also come with responsibility. Bangladesh still have work to do to become a consistently competitive Test side.
In addition, cricket as we know it in Bangladesh requires an overhaul, and it must begin with better domestic cricket.
Pitches must also encourage skill development rather than short‑term results, and young players must be groomed for the demands of five‑day cricket, not just white‑ball formats. Fitness standards, workload management, and long‑term planning must all improve.
This win is a milestone, but it can and should also be a turning point. We can compete with the best in the toughest conditions. Now we must build on it and make it a habit.

Investing in science. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The development of a new diagnostic kit for fish diseases by Bangladeshi researchers is an encouraging reminder of what local scientific innovation can achieve.
Such a breakthrough is practical and one that can help farmers detect infections early, reduce losses, and ultimately strengthen a sector that feeds millions.
However, we must look at this as a symbol of something larger: Bangladesh’s potential when science is taken seriously, funded consistently, and treated as a pillar of national development rather than an afterthought.
For too long, scientific research in Bangladesh has operated on limited budgets, fragmented support, and inconsistent policy attention. Yet every time researchers deliver - whether through agricultural innovation, medical devices, climate‑resilient crops, or environmental monitoring - the impact is immediate and tangible.
The fish‑disease diagnostic kit is one such example: A locally developed tool addressing a local problem with direct benefits for farmers, food security, and the economy.
Bangladesh needs far more of this. Science must not be treated as a luxury but as the foundation of resilience, especially for a developing nation such as ours.
As climate impacts intensify, as public health challenges grow, as food systems strain, and as industries demand new skills, we cannot rely on imported solutions alone. We must build our own scientific capacity.
That will not be possible without sustained investment. Research funding must be predictable, not sporadic and young scientists must have career pathways that encourage innovation rather than push them out of the country. Most importantly, scientific achievements must be integrated into national planning, not celebrated briefly and forgotten.
Investing in science is essential for a country seeking stability, competitiveness, and long‑term prosperity. It is time to support researchers, fund innovation, and make science central to national development.

item.title: Having humane healthcare. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Prime minister Tarique Rahman’s inauguration of the new 500‑bed building at the National Institute of Neurosciences & Hospital (NINS) is certainly a welcome addition to Bangladesh’s strained healthcare infrastructure. With that said, it is the PM’s emphasis on a humane, patient‑centred approach which is arguably the more important takeaway for the long-term.
In a system where overcrowding, long waits, and uneven service quality remain all-too-common, compassion from all involved in the medical sector in our country has long been the missing component and is increasingly a necessity.
However, while this new facility is a positive step, we must also be cognizant of the fact that Bangladesh’s healthcare system needs far more support, investment, and reform to meet the needs of its people.
Infrastructure expansion is essential, but buildings alone cannot fix systemic gaps. Bangladesh needs more skilled doctors, nurses, technicians, and administrators, and this skill must not just be technical but also in ensuring they understand the honour of being of service to people.
Equally critical is strengthening primary healthcare across the nation, as too many patients need to travel to Dhaka for conditions that should be treated locally, straining hospitals in the capital while leaving rural populations underserved.
Affordability remains another challenge. Even when services exist, many families struggle with the cost of treatment, tests, and medicines. A humane healthcare system must protect citizens from financial hardship, not push them into it.
Quality and accountability must also improve. Patients deserve clean wards, functioning equipment, timely diagnostics, and respectful treatment. These ought to be basic standards in our medical institutions and not luxuries that can only be afforded by the privileged in private hospitals and clinics.
The PM’s call for humane care is the right message and must be heeded. Achieving this goal requires a system capable of delivering humane care everywhere, not just in a few facilities.

There is no alternative to proper banking. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
We really do need a functional banking system more than we need money. Or to say the same thing another way, people really have stolen a lot of the money from the banking system.
But we're going to have to just grin and pay up -- because having the banking system is much more important to us than waiting until we can make the thieves pay it all back.
This is not what we would like. It is also, sadly, true.
The governor of the Bank of Bangladesh -- the central bank -- has said : “Nearly one-third of the total money in bank loans has practically been stolen.”
The way that banking works, this means that nearly one-third of the money that we have deposited in banks has been stolen. Yes, banks have capital as well, but one third is much more than they have of that.
So, now the banks have no capital and also have lost some portion of all the deposits that were made into them.
This is not true of every bank. Some are vastly worse than others. But banks are, overall, a system. Loss of confidence in a part of the system could -- and today does -- mean loss in the system as a whole.
We've had reports of people withdrawing their cash from the banks and keeping it as cash outside the banks. This is perfectly sensible. It's also, in itself, a disaster for the wider economy.
For banks -- assuming the money isn't all stolen -- perform a duty. They recycle peoples' savings into investment.
The cash that we put aside, as long as it's in a bank, produces the working capital that a company needs to be able to trade.
Or the mortgage so that someone can buy an apartment. Or....well, whatever it is that people borrow money for.
Our deposits into banks finance the loans banks make. So, if we're not willing to deposit, then loans are not made and the economy stutters, slows, and we gain no economic growth.
In fact, when this happened in the 1930s in the US, the economy shrank by 25% in only a couple of years. We would not like this to happen to us today.
The central bank knows this and is doing what a central bank should : “To prevent systemic defaults, Bangladesh Bank has injected over Tk76,000 crore in emergency liquidity support into fragile institutions.”
For, yes, we are very annoyed (to put it mildly) that the thefts of the loans occurred but overall, it's better that we keep the banks going than that we don't keep the banks going.
Annoying as that is, it's just the way it all works out. Having a banking system is better than not having a banking system.
We are, and I'm sorry about this, simply going to have to pay to keep the banks solvent -- to stop them from going bust.
Yes, it's true that the money was stolen and that's not our fault but we're still going to have to pay.
Simply because still having banks taking deposits and making loans is more valuable to us than not having it.
That is not where it stops. We will then have to make sure that the new politics do not lead to it just being a new group who can get loans they can steal.
We also need to hold those who did steal accountable. The bank shareholders, who allowed this to happen, should lose their money. The bank management should all be fired. If we can, we should steal their pensions.
Those who took the loans and are not repaying -- we bankrupt them. If the money's in flats and houses in London, then we pursue them to Britain and take those flats and houses. We do not let them get away with this.
A major reason we must not let them get away with it is so that no one tries this again. We really do want those who have stolen from the banks to end up trying to sell tea outside a metro station. Pursue them to the ends of the Earth.
But, all that said, we are going to have to pay to recapitalize those banks.
And, if we need to in order to maintain confidence in the banking system itself, then, as taxpayers, we are going to have to pay back those depositors whose money was stolen.
I'm sorry about this, I really am. But the value to us as an economy of still having a banking system is so great that we, us out here, are going to have to carry the costs of those thefts.
We should -- must -- punish those who stole and we might get some of the money back as we do so. But save banking first, then punish the thieves.

A nation faltering at the wheel. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The latest July data from the Road Safety Foundation (RSF) brought no surprises, only a familiar but tragic reality.
The organization counted 416 people killed and 629 injured in 458 crashes across Bangladesh. Coming right after June's toll of 438, the country lost 854 lives in just two months.
Yet, these shocking figures caused barely a ripple in the national conversation.
Somewhere inside those two months, at a United Nations high-level meeting on road safety in July, Bangladesh restated its commitments on halving road deaths and injuries by 2030 and enacting a comprehensive road safety law by December 2027.
The pledge was made abroad while the July toll was accumulating at home.
Around the time the March Eid-rush was filling our highways, a smaller and far less dramatic vehicle arrived in Singapore.
It is a 16-seater electric bus , studded with cameras and sensors that give it a complete 360-degree view of its surroundings. It has no steering wheel, no pedals, and no human driver who can lose patience, experience fatigue, or take a reckless move to overtake a rival on a blind curve.
Land Transport Authority (LTA) received the first of six autonomous buses that will enter public service as part of a three-year pilot in mid-2026. Before the bus touches a public road, it will be put through rigorous closed-circuit testing , a stark contrast to the untested, unfit vehicles routinely deployed on Bangladeshi highways.
The price of a deadly status quo
The contrast with our own roads is not subtle. According to RSF, at least 274 people were killed and over 1,500 injured in 342 accidents during the 10-day Eid-ul-Fitr travel window from March 16 to 26.
The deadliest single incident occurred when a passenger bus lost control and plunged into the Padma River from a pontoon at the Daulatdia ferry ghat, claiming 26 lives.
A mail train rammed into a passenger bus after sleeping gatekeepers failed to lower the security barriers, killing 12 more at a level crossing in Comilla.
By the end of March, the toll had climbed to 532 deaths and 2,221 injuries across 576 accidents during that month alone.
The fatalities continued unabated into April 2026, which recorded 404 deaths and 709 injuries from 463 crashes. This grim period seamlessly transitioned into the next holiday season.
During the 13-day Eid-ul-Adha travel period from May 21 to June 2, 2026, the country witnessed another wave of carnage. RSF reported 281 fatalities and 837 injuries in 292 road accidents nationwide during this rush, with motorcycles proving to be the deadliest mode of transport, accounting for 124 of those deaths.
Among the most devastating of these tragedies was an incident on May 25 in Tangail's Kalihati Upazila, where an overloaded cargo truck illegally carrying homebound passengers under a tarpaulin cover overturned into a roadside ditch, crushing 15 labourers to death .
These occurrences were far from unusual; they were the predictable outcomes of a system that has failed to protect people year after year, Eid after Eid.
Then the festivals ended, and the numbers did not move. That is the part worth sitting with. June and July carried no holiday rush and no seasonal excuse and still produced 854 deaths between them.
In July, motorcycle crashes killed 138 people, just over a third of the total. Pedestrians accounted for another 106. National highways, the stretches built for speed and supposedly the best engineered, hosted 169 of the month’s crashes. Loss of vehicle control was again the single largest cause.
A separate count published in late July, days before the eighth anniversary of the 2018 student road safety movement, found that 7,364 students had been killed on the roads between 2019 and June this year, more than 15% of all road deaths in that period.
Of those, 391 died in the first six months of 2026. The children who marched for safer roads in 2018 have been replaced on the casualty lists by children who were too young to march.
The overall picture is grim, with the RSF’s 2025 Eid data highlighting the specific catalysts of the crisis. Loss of control caused 44% of accidents, and head-on collisions made up 26%.
Motorcycles, which quadrupled from 1.5 million to over six million in a decade, accounted for more than 42% of all Eid fatalities .
Ultimately, behind almost every statistic lies an avoidable human error: An exhausted driver racing against the clock on a blind curve, or a desperate motorcyclist riding without a license or a helmet.
What is the real count?
There is a fundamental failure sitting underneath all of this. Bangladesh, it seems, cannot accurately track its own road fatalities.
For 2025, the Bangladesh Road Transport Authority (BRTA) recorded 5,490 deaths and called it the highest annual figure on record.
RSF, working from media reports, counted more than 7,300 .
The Bangladesh Jatri Kalyan Samity put it at 9,111 .
The World Health Organization, using modelled estimates, once placed the toll for a single earlier year at close to 32,000 while local counts for that same year sat below 8,000.
These are not variations at the margin. Between the lowest and the highest domestic count sits a gap larger than the entire annual road death toll of many if not most countries.
An agency cannot target what it cannot measure. Blackspot identification, budget allocation, and any honest test of whether a policy worked all rest on a number the state does not reliably possess.
Singapore will monitor six autonomous buses in real time and judge them against a defined standard. We cannot say within several thousand how many of our own citizens died last year, and no institution carries an obligation to reconcile the difference.
Dr Sabbir Ahmad, a tech executive with global experience in digital connectivity, sustainable infrastructure and energy, now shaping Bangladesh's semiconductor landscape as the CEO of Silicon Array Ltd. Email: sabbir@ieee.org .

Rampant Bangladesh make history with first-ever Test win in Australia. [ dawn ]
item.description:
A dominant Bangladesh stunned hosts Australia to win the first Test by nine wickets in Darwin on Sunday for a historic maiden Test victory on Australian soil.

After bowling Australia out for 284 and needing 57 to win, the visitors cruised past the total when Mominul Haque slashed Beau Webster to the backward point boundary.

Bangladesh dominated Australia throughout the match and the margin of victory will send shockwaves through the cricketing world.

After bowling Australia out for 198 in the first innings, the visitors always looked the more likely to win.

They kept the pressure on throughout Sunday and didn’t panic when Cameron Green (104) brought up his third Test century after lunch on day four.

Green was offered no real support from his teammates and the Bangladeshis kept taking vital scalps to leave Australia on the ropes, with Mehidy Hasan Miraz taking 5-66.

The visitors went into the match with most observers giving them no chance of winning.

Their only warm-up game, against a Cricket Australia XI, ended in a big loss that included a second-innings collapse where they were all out for 54.

But they have completely outplayed the Australians and won every session, batting, bowling and catching better than their more illustrious counterparts.

Australia, fielding their best possible team, have looked out of sorts from the beginning.

Their batting failed in the first innings when they were bowled out on the opening day, then their much-vaunted bowling attack struggled against the gritty Bangladesh batsmen.

Led by a maiden Test century from opener Tanzid Hasan, Bangladesh made 426 and importantly kept Australia in the field for 138 overs in Darwin’s heat and humidity.

The bowlers then showed great patience Saturday to make regular breakthroughs and keep Australia under the cosh.

When Australia resumed Sunday on 161-4, most of their hopes lay with Alex Carey and Green.

Carey lived dangerously in the opening 30 minutes, twice edging seamer Hasan Mahmud through the vacant slips cordon for boundaries.

But on 30 Mehidy produced a beautiful ball, pitching in line then turning sharply to take Carey’s outside edge to wicketkeeper Litton Das.

He struck again soon after, bowling Webster for five to leave Australia 193-6 and in deep trouble.

A famous victory edged ever closer when Australia captain Pat Cummins pushed forward to a Mehidy delivery and got an inside edge to short leg, where Shadman Islam took a sharp chance.

Australia were 207-7, still 21 runs behind Bangladesh’s first-innings total.

Green and Mitchell Starc batted sensibly to ensure Bangladesh had to bat again.

Starc fell for 18 caught behind but Green was playing well and brought up his century shortly after lunch.

But despite looking increasingly comfortable, he was undone when a Hasan ball kept low, hit the toe end of his bat and cannoned into the stumps.

Mehidy wrapped up the innings when he trapped Nathan Lyon plumb in front leg before.

Depsite losing Tanzid in the first over, Mominul and Shadman Islam cruised to victory.
